RMediation Technical Notes

Source: vignettes/articles/technical-notes.Rmd
technical-notes.Rmd

Why these behaviors work the way they do. Each section states the rule, the reason, and where it is tested.

1. pprodnormal3() uses Gauss-Legendre by default

Rule. pprodnormal3(method = "gauss") is the default: tensor-product Gauss-Legendre quadrature on a domain split at the coordinate axes, with the node count increased until successive rules agree to tol.

Reason. The adaptive "hcubature" method returned silently wrong values on an ill-conditioned covariance matrix: 24% error at a correlation of 0.999 (up to 92% relative in the lower tail), and exactly 0 at large standardized means. It is kept only for cross-checking.

cv <- diag(c(0.05, 0.04, 0.03)^2)
p <- pprodnormal3(0.1, mean = c(0.4, 0.5, 0.6), cov = cv, diagnostics = TRUE)
c(probability = as.numeric(p), error = attr(p, "error"), nodes = attr(p, "nodes"))
#>  probability        error        nodes 
#> 1.422054e-01 1.387779e-16 2.560000e+02

Two details look like bugs and are not. The truncation bound is derived from a tail-mass argument, not tuned, because truncation error is a bias and a self-consistency check cannot see a bias. The domain splits at 0 even when the mean lies beyond the bound; one cell then has reversed limits and negative weights, and the two cells telescope to the intended box.

2. mbco() and OpenMx’s dropped constraint (OpenMx#433)

The problem. OpenMx silently drops an equality constraint whose Jacobian is exactly zero at the starting values (OpenMx/OpenMx#433). A product constraint a*b == 0 started at a = b = 0 is such a constraint: the null model is fitted without it, so the statistic is 0 with a status of 0.

What mbco() does. After fitting, mbco() checks h0 for a violated constraint. It warns (RMediation_constraint_violation), refits h0 at a tighter feasibility tolerance, and uses the refit statistic. If the refit cannot repair the violation, the call stops (RMediation_h0_refit_failed) rather than return an understated number.

Why the warning is named “not enforced”. When h0’s fit equals h1’s fit although a constraint was violated, mbco() signals RMediation_constraint_not_enforced. A fitted h0 keeps no starting values, so the function cannot tell a dropped constraint from a violation that OpenMx accepted within its feasibility tolerance (default 0.05). The name and the message say only what is observable: the constraint may not have been enforced.

What to use for a product null. mbco_product_null() fixes one path at 0 per branch, runs mbco() on each, and returns the branch with the largest p-value. A test of a union of nulls rejects only if every single-path null is rejected (an intersection-union test), and fixing a parameter is exact, so neither the dropped-constraint problem nor the wrong-branch problem arises.

3. The bootstrap p-value and failed replicates

Rule. For type = "semi" and type = "parametric", the p-value is the proportion of kept replicate statistics strictly above the observed statistic:

p=#{kept replicates with T*>Tobs}#{kept replicates}p = \frac{\#\{\text{kept replicates with } T^* > T_{\text{obs}}\}}{\#\{\text{kept replicates}\}}

There is no +1 correction. This is the rule OpenMx’s mxCompare(boot = TRUE) used.

Dropped replicates. A replicate whose OpenMx fit did not converge is dropped, up to 5% of R; exactly 5% is allowed. Above that the call stops with RMediation_bootstrap_too_many_dropped. The count is reported in result@dropped. With fewer than 20 replicates a single drop already exceeds 5%.

What is never dropped. A replicate whose constraint violation cannot be repaired stops the call (RMediation_bootstrap_infeasible), as do a non-finite or a negative statistic. An infeasible fit understates the statistic, so it is not a draw from the null distribution, and dropping it would bias the p-value downward.

Example of the arithmetic. With 100 replicates, 4 dropped, 24 of the 96 kept above the observed value, and 10 of the kept tied with it: p = 24 / 96 = 0.25. A denominator of 100 would give 0.24, and >= would count the ties and give 34 / 96. The package tests pin this case.

4. The exact CDF of a product of two normals, and its perfectly correlated case

Rule. pprodnormal() and qprodnormal() with type = "dop" compute the CDF of a*b by one-dimensional integration of the bivariate normal (Meeker and Escobar, 1994). When |rho| = 1 the two factors are linear in one standard normal variable, so a*b is a quadratic in it and the CDF has a closed form from the roots of that quadratic. The package uses the closed form, not a step integral.

Reason. A step integral at |rho| = 1 was off by up to 4.3e-5 and once stopped with “probably divergent”. The closed form is exact, and every one of the 495 evaluations in the article’s test domain now succeeds.

set.seed(1)
z <- rnorm(2e6)
a <- 0.3 + 0.2 * z   # mu.x = 0.3, se.x = 0.2
b <- 0.5 + 0.1 * z   # mu.y = 0.5, se.y = 0.1, perfectly correlated with a
q <- c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30)
rbind(
  exact      = pprodnormal(q, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, rho = 1),
  simulation = vapply(q, function(v) mean(a * b <= v), 0)
)
#>                 [,1]     [,2]      [,3]
#> exact      0.1863292 0.500000 0.8413447
#> simulation 0.1863300 0.499953 0.8412675

The exact row and the simulated row agree to Monte Carlo error (about 3 decimals at this sample size).

5. Point masses: a zero standard error

Rule. A factor with zero standard error is a constant, so the product is either a constant or a scaled normal. pprodnormal() returns the exact answer there, and the CDF of a point mass is right-continuous: at an atom at q, P(X <= q) = 1.

Reason. A CDF is right-continuous by definition. Earlier versions returned 0.5 at an atom at 0, which is the midpoint convention, not a CDF. The change is in NEWS as a behavior change.

c(at_atom = pprodnormal(0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  just_below = pprodnormal(-1e-9, 0, 0, 0, 0))
#>    at_atom just_below 
#>          1          0

# One fixed factor: the product is normal(mu.x * mu.y, (mu.x * se.y)^2)
c(pprodnormal = pprodnormal(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0, 0.1),
  normal      = pnorm(0.1, mean = 0.3 * 0.5, sd = 0.3 * 0.1))
#> pprodnormal      normal 
#>  0.04779035  0.04779035

pprodnormal3() follows the same rule with two or three zero-variance components (issue #64).

6. The densities

Rule. dprodnormal() is the exact density of the product of two normals, and dprodnormal3() of three. For two normals with zero means the density is a Bessel K0 expression; otherwise it is a one-dimensional integral (Rohatgi; Glen). The three-factor density is a one-dimensional integral of the two-factor density conditioned on the first factor. At exactly 0 the density is infinite for zero means, and dprodnormal() returns Inf there.

Reason. A closed form exists only for the zero-mean case. The integral form is exact up to the integration tolerance. At ordinary scales it agrees with a finite difference of the CDF, as below. At very small standard errors a CDF difference is the noisier side (it divides the CDF’s own absolute error by a tiny step), so the tests there use an independent oracle: direct quadrature of the conditioning integral, or, when one factor is nearly constant, the density of the remaining factors scaled by that factor’s mean.

h <- 1e-5
c(density = dprodnormal(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1),
  numerical_derivative =
    (pprodnormal(0.1 + h, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1) -
     pprodnormal(0.1 - h, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1)) / (2 * h))
#>              density numerical_derivative 
#>             3.719755             3.719755

Narrow spike. When a factor’s mean is very large relative to its standard error (mu / se above about 3000 for two factors, about 1000 for some three-factor inner integrals), the integrand is a narrow spike. Before 1.9.0 a fixed window around the mean missed it, so dprodnormal() and dprodnormal3() could return 0, NA or a silently low value (#117). The integration window is now split at the spike, found from the roots of the conditional mean, and subintervals far from it retry with an absolute tolerance scaled to the peak. Values at ordinary scales are unchanged.
